evaluation.positioning_hook: A star basketball player rebuilds her life in a Missouri-to-Pennsylvania journey of grief, faith, and second chances, where a cemetery promise and a small-town gym lead her to love.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is clear and accessible: grief, healing, faith, basketball, and romance all have recognizable audience lanes. The challenge is that the script plays in a softer, faith-forward, small-town register rather than a broad commercial engine, so the audience is real but not explosive.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands cleanly once the story reveals the cemetery promise and the return to Pottsville to bury Frank and Beth together. The hook is strongest in the back half, where the basketball comeback and the romance converge, but the opening section takes time to reveal the actual feature engine.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Skylar is a strong lead: elite, wounded, and emotionally legible, with a clear arc from athlete to mentor to woman choosing a life. Ralph is also appealing as a restrained, service-oriented romantic lead, and Maddie gives the story a warm family anchor.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s blend of women’s basketball, faith, funeral ritual, and small-town romance gives it a distinct lane, especially in the Pottsville church/cemetery material. The execution, though, is largely familiar in its emotional beats and leans on well-worn inspirational-drama rhythms.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The basketball set pieces and the cemetery journey create momentum, and the injury-to-recovery-to-return structure gives the feature a clear spine. Still, the middle stretches are episodic and reflective, with several scenes functioning more as emotional waypoints than escalating turns.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea of a WNBA star returning to a small town to fulfill a burial promise is fresh enough to feel ownable, and the church/school-district world adds texture. What keeps it from a higher score is that the emotional logic is straightforward and the story’s surprises are modest.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Pottsville, St. Andrew’s Church, the school district, and the local gym create a lived-in, story-generating environment with clear social roles and routines. The world feels specific without becoming complicated, and the church-school-basketball ecosystem gives the script a stable identity.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is consistent and recognizable: sincere, faith-inflected, and gently romantic, with sports-movie uplift. The cemetery scenes, church interiors, and dance-floor payoff give it a clear emotional register, even if the tonal palette is not especially surprising.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material in grief, vocation, and the tension between ambition and rootedness, especially in Skylar’s injury and Ralph’s fear of opening up again. The script mostly states those themes plainly rather than layering them with much ambiguity or subtext.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Skylar/Ralph/Maddie is a solid triangle, and the family and church relationships add recurring emotional pressure. The ensemble is not sprawling, but the key relationships are functional and generate enough scene-to-scene energy to carry the feature.

lead_characters.name: Skylar Monroe
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late teens to late 20s; elite basketball player; Midwestern; emotionally guarded but warm; likely white.
lead_characters.hook: Skylar is a gifted, high-pressure athlete who starts as a championship-level scorer and ends as a woman forced to rebuild her identity after injury. She carries grief, ambition, and tenderness in the same frame, and the script gives her a credible evolution from star to mentor to someone choosing love and home on her own terms.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a sports-drama lead like Auliʻi Cravalho in 'The Power' or Queen Latifah in 'Bessie'—a role that lets an actor play physical command, emotional collapse, and quiet authority in one arc.

lead_characters.name: Ralph
lead_characters.demographics: Man, late 30s to early 40s; widower; church/school-district worker; father; working-class; likely white.
lead_characters.hook: Ralph is the grounded small-town widower whose life is built on duty, routine, and restraint until Skylar pulls him back into the possibility of wanting more. He’s written as a man of quiet decency with real emotional history, and the script uses his hesitation as part of the romance rather than a stall.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of restrained, emotionally loaded work that gave Ben Mendelsohn in 'The Outsider' or Michael Shannon in 'Take Shelter' room to play interior damage, steadiness, and a late-blooming romantic pulse.

lead_characters.name: Maddie
lead_characters.demographics: Girl, 8-14 across the story; Ralph’s daughter; basketball player; observant, earnest, and emotionally perceptive.
lead_characters.hook: Maddie is the kid who sees more than adults expect and becomes the bridge between Skylar’s past and future. She’s not just cute support; she has agency in the school-gym material, moral clarity in the coach conflict, and real emotional function in the family structure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong young-performer material in the lane of Brooklynn Prince in 'The Florida Project'—a role that gives a child actor specificity, emotional intelligence, and scenes that matter to the adult story.

lead_characters.name: Beth Rose
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 60s to 70s; grandmother; devout, warm, emotionally articulate.
lead_characters.hook: Beth is the story’s spiritual and emotional keeper, the one who links the basketball legacy, the marriage story, and the burial promise. Even in limited scenes, she functions as the script’s moral compass and the keeper of the title’s emotional thesis.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-career showcase that gives Frances McDormand in 'Nomadland' or June Squibb in 'Nebraska' the chance to be both plainspoken and devastatingly specific.

lead_characters.name: Frank Rose
lead_characters.hook: Frank is the quiet patriarch whose presence is felt most strongly through memory, ritual, and the way the family talks about him after death. He’s less a plot engine than an emotional inheritance, but the script uses him effectively as the voice that keeps returning in Skylar’s head.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Richard Jenkins did in 'The Visitor'—project warmth, authority, and memory with very little screen time.

lead_characters.name: Jason
lead_characters.demographics: Man, late 20s to early 30s; supportive ex/partner; emotionally steady, urban-adjacent, grounded.
lead_characters.hook: Jason is the clean, decent relationship that Skylar can’t quite keep once her life changes shape. He’s written less as a villain than as the emotional contrast that clarifies what Skylar is choosing, which makes him useful and credible even when he’s not the endgame.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of emotionally intelligent breakup role that gave Adam Brody in 'The Kid Detective' or John Krasinski in 'A Quiet Place' a chance to play decency under pressure and still leave a mark.

lead_characters.name: Coach Wensil
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s; high school coach; blunt, observant, community-minded.
lead_characters.hook: Coach Wensil is the practical adult who recognizes talent and gives Skylar a place to redirect it. He’s a functional but useful supporting role, especially once the story shifts from romance to mentorship and community leadership.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded authority role that lets an actor work in the lane of J.K. Simmons in 'Whiplash' or Craig T. Nelson in 'Parenthood'—blunt, funny, and quietly pivotal.

lead_characters.name: Katie Clarkson
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 20s; elite basketball player; electric, fearless.
lead_characters.hook: Katie is the new-generation player who pulls Skylar back toward the game and gives the later basketball material a fresh competitive edge. She’s more functional than deeply explored, but she helps keep the sports world alive after Skylar’s injury.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of high-energy supporting athlete role that gives an actor the snap and confidence of Hailee Steinfeld in 'Bumblebee'—fast, charismatic, and scene-lifting.

lead_characters.name: Coach Green
lead_characters.hook: Coach Green is the steady professional presence in the Fever material, the person who keeps the team coherent when Skylar’s injury blows the season apart. She’s not deeply individualized, but she gives the pro-basketball sections authority and structure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of efficient, authoritative role that lets an actor play the grounded leadership of Viola Davis in 'Air'—command without overstatement.

lead_characters.name: Sharon Maid
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 40s; church office administrator; warm, efficient.
lead_characters.hook: Sharon is the kind of support character who makes the church world feel operational rather than symbolic. She’s a small but useful texture role, giving the Pottsville setting a lived-in institutional feel.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of role that can give a character actor the easy specificity of Amy Ryan in 'Win Win'—brief, natural, and memorable without needing a big speech.

lead_characters.name: Father Phillips
lead_characters.hook: Father Phillips functions as the script’s faith voice and moral framing device, especially in the burial and romantic decision scenes. He’s not complex on the page, but he gives the story a clear spiritual register and helps the ending land with ceremony.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of dignified supporting role that gives an actor the measured authority of Tom Wilkinson in 'The Full Monty'—a calm center with a few well-placed lines.

lead_characters.name: Lisa Monroe
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, mid-20s; older sister; family support.
lead_characters.hook: Lisa is a functional family presence who helps round out the Monroe household and gives Skylar a sibling witness to the draft and grief material. She’s underwritten relative to the lead, but she helps the family scenes feel less isolated.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supportive family role that can give an actor the grounded utility of Merritt Wever in 'Marriage Story'—present, specific, and emotionally legible.

lead_characters.name: Tim Moss
lead_characters.hook: Tim is the school-system adult who can move things forward once the gym and coaching worlds intersect. He’s a clean utility role, but he helps the school setting feel administratively real.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of compact authority role that gives an actor the functional presence of Bob Balaban in 'Lady Bird'—small, specific, and useful.

lead_characters.name: Lindsey Hill
lead_characters.hook: Lindsey is part of the later team engine and helps the pro-basketball sections feel like a real unit rather than a two-character setup. She’s more ensemble support than standalone character, but she contributes to the team texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of ensemble athlete role that gives an actor the easy, lived-in energy of a supporting player in 'Friday Night Lights'—team-first but still visible.

lead_characters.name: Lyla Nevada
lead_characters.hook: Lyla is another piece of the team fabric, especially in the injury and comeback material where Skylar’s leadership is defined by how the others respond to her. She’s not deeply individualized, but she helps the team feel populated.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of ensemble role that gives an actor the utility and presence of a recurring sports teammate in 'One Tree Hill' or 'Friday Night Lights'.

lead_characters.name: Casey Middletown
lead_characters.hook: Casey rounds out the later team and helps the script sell the idea of a real roster, not just a star and a few placeholders. She’s functional, but she contributes to the sports-world credibility.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of team-role that gives an actor a clean, professional sports-drama lane—small but useful, with room to feel part of a winning unit.

casting_characteristics: One child role with meaningful emotional continuity across ages 8-14
Supporting cast includes multiple age-specific adult roles
Athletic ensemble for pro and high-school basketball sequences

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond scoreboard graphics and crowd enhancement if desired.
technical.sfx_needs: Basketball game choreography, injury fall, crowd/arena atmosphere, funeral and burial practicals.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; emotional sports-romance drama with faith and family appeal

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the script includes multiple basketball game environments, arena crowd scenes, a hospital sequence, a road-trip stretch, and a dance-floor finale that all benefit from scale.

casting.note: The lead needs to credibly play an elite basketball star across injury, recovery, and romance, while Maddie must carry meaningful emotional continuity from child to early teen. Several supporting roles also need authentic athletic or institutional presence.

development.note: The burial promise, injury recovery, and romance all track cleanly, but the script’s emotional center shifts from sports to grief to romance to mentorship, which makes the buyer conversation about primary hook and audience lane important.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult viewers who respond to inspirational sports dramas, faith-adjacent family stories, and romance with a strong emotional payoff.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 30+, with a meaningful female audience and family-viewing appeal; strongest with viewers who like character-first sports stories.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary feature with a modest location footprint, but basketball games, arena atmospherics, and a dance-finale sequence keep it above micro.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams building adult female uplift
specialty distributors seeking faith-friendly crossover titles
indie producers in the sports-drama lane
buyers looking for family-safe emotional crowd-pleasers
lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the lane of character-first inspirational drama: sports as the engine, grief as the wound, romance as the release, and faith as the framing device. It is commercially legible to buyers who want uplift without going full Hallmark and who can market around a recognizable athletic lead.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the story resolves Skylar’s emotional and romantic arc cleanly, and there is no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond the central relationship.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Skylar is a true star role.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a clear casting and marketing center: a lead who can sell athletic authority, grief, and romantic vulnerability in one package. That is attractive to female-star vehicles and to buyers looking for a performance-forward sports drama.
strengths.evidence: The championship shot, the injury collapse, the hospital breakdown, and the final choice to stay in Pottsville all belong to Skylar’s emotional arc.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The burial promise gives the story a clean spine.
strengths.what_it_means: The ashes-to-Pottsville journey creates a simple, emotionally legible engine that can be marketed in one sentence and understood immediately by audiences. That clarity helps the script travel to buyers who want a heartfelt, high-concept emotional premise without genre confusion.
strengths.evidence: Beth’s request to return Frank and Beth’s ashes to their plots in St. Anthony’s Cemetery drives the entire second half.

strengths.what_it_means: The setting gives the film a recognizable small-town ecosystem with built-in institutions, rituals, and visual identity. That kind of texture helps a modestly budgeted feature feel bigger and more lived-in than its footprint.
strengths.evidence: St. Andrew’s Church, South Schuylkill schools, the cemetery, and the gym all recur as meaningful spaces rather than generic backdrops.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ralph and Maddie add a family engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The father-daughter dynamic broadens the emotional appeal beyond romance and gives the film a second audience entry point. That makes the project more attractive to buyers who want a family-safe emotional hook alongside the sports material.
strengths.evidence: Ralph’s routines with Maddie, her basketball arc, and his protective response to her coach conflict create recurring relational stakes.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending payoff is clean and marketable.
strengths.what_it_means: The final dance and kiss deliver a satisfying emotional release that buyers can easily understand as the movie’s signature moment. That kind of ending helps trailers, posters, and audience word-of-mouth because the title concept and payoff align neatly.
strengths.evidence: The spring dance sequence culminates in Skylar’s line that all she needs is one dance, followed by the title card return.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, emotionally legible female-led sports-romance with a strong star vehicle at its center and a modest, controllable production footprint. The burial promise, church/gym world, and final dance payoff give buyers a clear market identity: inspirational, faith-adjacent, and performance-driven without needing franchise scale.

items.detail: The script moves from championship sports story to grief drama to burial-road-trip to romance to mentorship, and each mode is workable on its own. The buyer conversation will be about which of those is the actual hook, because the feature currently asks the audience to track several different promises at once.

items.area: The middle plays more episodic than escalating.
items.detail: Several stretches are built around reflective scenes, phone calls, and routine work rather than turns that force new decisions. That makes the script feel emotionally steady, but it also softens the sense of propulsion between the injury and the final dance payoff.

items.area: The basketball world is broad but not deep.
items.detail: The Fever and high-school sequences give the film scale, but the team members beyond Skylar and Katie are mostly functional names and reactions. For a sports feature, that means the ensemble energy is serviceable rather than memorable, and the game-world specificity is lighter than the premise suggests.

items.area: The romance is clean, but not especially surprising.
items.detail: Ralph is appealing and the chemistry is gentle, but the relationship follows a familiar wounded-widow / wounded-athlete path. That makes it easy to root for, though it also means the film’s differentiation will depend more on tone and setting than on romantic unpredictability.

items.area: Named brands and music need a legal pass.
items.detail: The script explicitly names the Phoenix Mercury, Indiana Fever, New York Liberty, Gainbridge Fieldhouse, and Shania Twain’s 'From This Moment On.' Those are manageable clearance items, but they are real line items that need to be addressed before a buyer treats the package as clean.

issues.headline: The script is commercially legible, but it asks buyers to choose between several emotional engines: sports comeback, grief ritual, and small-town romance. The other main friction is practical rather than creative — the basketball scale is modestly expensive, and the named sports/music references will need a business affairs pass.
